source.title: Scaling Laws of Synthetic Images for Model Training … for Now
source.authors: Lijie Fan; Kaifeng Chen; Dilip Krishnan; Dina Katabi; Phillip Isola; Yong-Long Tian

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in image-classifier and CLIP training, extending the scaling-law question to synthetic-image data and vision models. It also reports that scaling depends on generation settings and that curves bend when model capacity is insufficient.
record.gate_note: The study scales training-image or image-text dataset size, not language-model parameter count or training compute. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, predict larger runs from small-run fits, or compare architecture shapes at fixed parameter count. The OOD, prompt, CFG, model-family, and dataset-scale results below are included where the paper reports an outcome relevant to image-scaling behavior. The paper also reports many individual prompts, CFG values, classes, and downstream tasks; aggregate statements and the reported 15-task average are used where available.
record.test_reason: The study fits log-loss against log-dataset-size (Eq. 2) for ViT image classifiers and CLIP models trained on synthetic and real images. It reports where the power-law form holds and where it bends. This bears on V5 (power-law form in other modalities) in a new setting. Only data size is scaled; there are no language models and no compute-optimal or architecture-at-fixed-size tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. After tuning text-to-image model, CFG and prompts, synthetic data scale slightly less effectively than real data for CLIP and significantly worse for supervised ImageNet classifiers. The authors attribute this mainly to text-to-image models failing to generate certain concepts. Power-law scaling holds until model capacity or compute limits, about 4M images supervised and about 64M captions for CLIP. Synthetic data help when real data are scarce, for OOD evaluation, in some classes, and when mixed with real data in CLIP.
record.recipe_differences: Vision rather than language models; scales synthetic-image or image-text dataset size and measures classification loss or zero-shot performance, not language-model held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling changes with prompt set, classifier-free guidance scale, text-to-image model, backbone capacity, evaluation domain, and CLIP training hyperparameter set.

fits_no_version.finding: On OOD sets with large domain shift (ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch), scaling synthetic data narrows the gap to real data and can surpass it at large scale (e.g. Muse). With 80 CLIP-template prompts the OOD advantage grows while in-domain scaling worsens. On ImageNet-v2, real data scale better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative scaling efficiency of synthetic versus real training data depends on the train–test domain gap.

record.problems: The results concern vision systems and training-data scale, not language-model parameter or compute scaling. The study attributes curve bending to capacity but states this as a hypothesis. Numerical exponents and uncertainty intervals for the main scaling curves are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports results for each of 15 downstream datasets at each scale; those individual dataset cells are omitted in favor of the table's reported Average column. Detailed per-prompt, per-CFG, per-class, and per-generator sweeps in Tables A4–A6 and figures in Sections 5 and Appendices C, G, and H are not enumerated individually. Figure 4 also plots ImageNet-A; the text does not describe a distinct outcome for that condition.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating small-run fits to much larger runs; no prediction is tested.
Effect of shape at fixed parameter count; only ViT-B versus ViT-L capacity is varied.
Scaling in model size or compute in vision (only dataset size is scaled), plus video, repeated data and fine-tuning regimes.
Downstream predictability for language models, from scale or pretraining loss.
Fitting-choice and setup dependence of language-model laws (parameter counting, schedules, fitting method, Kaplan versus Hoffmann disagreement).

missing.what: CLIP zero-shot ImageNet loss departs from the power law above about 64M captions. This is implied by 'under around 64 million' and shown in the plot up to 371M. Note the hyperparameter switch at 100M.
missing.locator: Section 6.2, Figure 9; Appendix B.1/H.1, Table A3

missing.what: CLIP zero-shot loss on the downstream average versus data scale (loss rather than accuracy), and per-dataset loss curves
missing.locator: Appendix H.3, Figures A14 and A15

missing.what: Table 1 omits the 32M, 64M and 256M rows and the ImageNet zero-shot column; these appear in Table A12
Per-class scaling: some 'Scaling' classes have synthetic k exceeding real; 'Poor' classes barely scale
Linear-probe accuracy of supervised classifiers on 15 datasets versus scale. It plateaus around 4–8M, e.g. SD CFG 7.5 Classname.

record.verdict_notes: The V7 and V6 links were removed because those versions concern language-model laws. Data-generation dependence of k and the curve bend are recorded instead as V5 scope limits for vision. Supervised training iterations scale with log dataset size, and CLIP switches hyperparameter sets at 100M captions; both shape the curves. No exponents or uncertainties are given in the text; k appears only in figures. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including the relative growth rates of model size and data.
Architecture effects at a fixed parameter count; the paper changes backbone capacity in a dataset-scaling experiment, not depth and width at fixed size.
Tests synthetic images in supervised classification and CLIP, including zero-shot transfer evaluation. Does not test video, repeated data, or fine-tuning as scaling regimes.
Reports downstream zero-shot classification performance across training-data scales; does not test the relation between downstream performance and language-model pretraining loss.

Shows sensitivity to image-generation configuration and a capacity-related bend in image scaling curves. Does not test language-model parameter-counting choices, compute-optimal splits, or disagreement between the Kaplan and Hoffmann compute-optimal laws.

rows.subject: ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on synthetic ImageNet images
rows.operation_detail: Sweep training dataset size and measure ImageNet validation loss.

conditions.value: synthetic images; configurations aggregated in the authors' statement

rows.measure: ImageNet validation cross-entropy loss versus dataset size
rows.value: The paper states that validation loss and training-data size are linearly related in log space from 0.125 million to 4 million training images.
rows.note: The text describes a power-law relationship over this range; no numerical exponent is stated here.
rows.check: Drop the V7 link. V7 concerns how published language-model laws depend on fitting and setup choices, and this is a vision data-scaling result. The state is correct: loss is linear in log space from 0.125M to 4M images.

rows.subject: ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on real ImageNet training images
rows.operation_detail: Compare loss scaling with real images against synthetic-image training.
rows.measure: Relative scaling ability of ImageNet validation loss with dataset size
rows.value: The paper states that real images typically have greater scaling ability than synthetic images.
rows.note: This compares the scaling slopes; the paper says optimized synthetic configurations still scale less effectively than real data.
rows.check: The baseline is the synthetic-data curve, and the row compares slopes (k), not whether a power law holds. Real-image ViT-B loss also follows the fitted power law, with steeper k. 'Partial' wrongly treats a smaller exponent for synthetic data as a weaker form. Drop V7.

rows.subject: ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on synthetic ImageNet images
rows.operation_detail: Compare scaling curves for default versus tuned image-generation prompts and CFG settings.

conditions.value: default prompt sets and CFG scales

rows.measure: ImageNet validation-loss scaling ability
rows.value: The paper states that default settings produce poor scaling ability, with a very flat slope and smaller k.
rows.note: The finding is about synthetic-image scaling and is explicitly conditional on generation settings.
rows.check: Drop V7. Default prompts and CFG give a 'very flat slope', so loss barely falls with data. The baseline is correctly the tuned settings.

rows.subject: ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on synthetic ImageNet images
rows.operation_detail: Scale synthetic data after tuning prompts and CFG settings.
rows.measure: ImageNet validation-loss scaling ability
rows.value: Tuning increases synthetic-data scaling and brings it closer to real-image scaling, but the best synthetic configuration remains significantly worse.
rows.note: The paper attributes the increase to greater diversity from tuned generation settings.
rows.check: Drop V7. With tuned settings the power law holds, but k stays 'significantly worse' than for real data. Partial is kept on the weaker-than-other-conditions rule.

rows.subject: ViT-B
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on synthetic images
rows.operation_detail: Extend the synthetic-image dataset-size sweep beyond 4 million images.
rows.measure: ImageNet validation loss versus dataset size
rows.value: The relationship changes above around 4 million images; validation loss in log space no longer exhibits a linear trend.
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that insufficient model capacity constrains the loss.
rows.check: Drop V7. Above about 4M images ViT-B loss leaves the log-linear trend. The authors only hypothesise that this is a capacity bottleneck, which would match the 'other factors not limiting' condition. Note that the Stable Diffusion curve extends to 64M.

rows.subject: ViT-L
rows.stage_stated: supervised classifier trained on synthetic images
rows.operation_detail: Increase backbone capacity and extend the dataset-size sweep.

conditions.value: best Stable Diffusion and Imagen configurations

rows.measure: ImageNet validation loss versus dataset size
rows.value: The paper states that ViT-L maintains a roughly linear ratio up to the 8 million scale and slightly postpones the inflection point.
rows.note: Increasing capacity delays, but does not establish the absence of, an inflection.
rows.check: Drop V7. With ViT-L the roughly linear log-log trend extends to 8M, which is consistent with the capacity explanation. The only shortfall is that the inflection is merely postponed, so observed is more accurate than partial.

rows.operation_detail: Measure the reported average zero-shot accuracy across 15 downstream datasets at increasing data scales.
rows.measure: Average zero-shot accuracy across 15 downstream datasets
rows.note: Table reports an aggregate mean over 15 datasets.
rows.check: This and R16–R35 are single accuracy cells at one scale. One accuracy value cannot show a power-law form, so 'observed' on each cell is meaningless. Across the cells, the averages rise monotonically with scale for all three data types. Table 1 also omits the 32M, 64M and 256M rows, which appear in Table A12. The V6 link proposed in the reader's label should not be applied, because V6 concerns language-model downstream predictability.

relationships.condition: ViT-B supervised classifiers on synthetic (0.125–4M) or real ImageNet images; ViT-L up to 8M; CLIP ViT-B on synthetic, real or combined LAION data below about 64M captions
relationships.reason: In these ranges, loss is linear against dataset size in log-log space (R1, R2, R6, R7, R8, R9).
relationships.display_finding: Loss was approximately linear against dataset size on log-log axes across the specified supervised and contrastive training ranges.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: ViT-B supervised classifiers on synthetic (0.125–4M) or real ImageNet images; ViT-L up to 8M; CLIP ViT-B on synthetic, real or combined LAION data below about 64M captions
source_check.reason: Sections 4.3–4.4 and 6.2 report approximately linear log-log loss scaling within these ranges.

relationships.condition: ViT-B supervised training beyond about 4M synthetic images
relationships.reason: Loss leaves the log-linear trend above about 4M (R5). The authors only hypothesise a capacity bottleneck, and ViT-L merely postpones the inflection (R6).
relationships.display_finding: ViT-B loss departed from its log-linear trend above approximately 4M synthetic images; ViT-L postponed the inflection, while a capacity bottleneck remained a hypothesis.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: ViT-B supervised training beyond about 4M synthetic images
source_check.reason: ViT-B departs from its log-log trend beyond approximately 4M images; ViT-L postpones the inflection. Insufficient capacity is hypothesized.

relationships.condition: Synthetic training data generated with default prompts/CFG versus tuned settings
relationships.reason: The exponent k depends strongly on how the data were generated. Default settings give a near-flat slope (R3), and even tuned synthetic data stay significantly below real-data k (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Default generation settings produced a near-flat scaling exponent, and tuned synthetic data still had substantially smaller exponents than real data.

source_check.condition: Synthetic training data generated with default prompts/CFG versus tuned settings
source_check.reason: Default settings produce much weaker scaling; tuning improves the slope, but supervised synthetic-image scaling remains significantly weaker than real-image scaling.

relation.reason: Its own dataset-size sweeps measure loss scaling and identify ranges where the power-law form holds or bends.

tranche.reason: Tests power-law data scaling in a new setting: supervised vision classifiers and CLIP trained with synthetic, real, or combined images.

source_check.notes: CLIP dataset size counts captions; combined training randomly selects a real or synthetic image per caption. Different exponents alone do not establish failure of the power-law form.

statements.correction: Default generation settings: shallow positive scaling. Tuned settings: improved scaling, weaker than real images. ViT-B: log-log trend changes above approximately 4M synthetic images. ViT-L: roughly linear trend extends to 8M, postponing the inflection. Capacity explanation: hypothesis. V5 verdict for these limitations: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The image-study facts are accurate, but its placement under challenges overstates the evidence: shallow scaling and a bend establish scope limitations, without demonstrating absent or reversed scaling.

reader_labels.reason: The paper explicitly reports power-law loss scaling in these image-training settings (R1, R7–R9).
